nightly-azure-canary.note: ITEM 2.3 (Wave 2, AI-OS research-pass 2026-07-21): schedule-liveness heartbeat for .github/workflows/nightly-azure-canary.yml (cron '20 8 * * *', daily). No `rg` here on purpose, this is a plain GitHub Actions cron, not a Container Apps Job, so there is nothing for heartbeat.mjs's ARM path to query; the workflow self-beats via `node setup/heartbeat.mjs beat nightly-azure-canary ok`, unconditionally, regardless of that workflow's OWN --strict verdict. That is deliberate: this heartbeat answers 'did the workflow's cron fire at all', a DIFFERENT failure class than 'did its content check go red' (GitHub disables a schedule after 60 days of repo inactivity; the workflow YAML could be deleted or malformed; a cron typo could make it never match, and none of that ever shows up as a red run, because a workflow that never runs never gets a chance to go red). 1560min = 26h gives a daily job one occasional-delay cycle of slack before it counts as LATE (heartbeat.mjs's own status math: LATE once age exceeds interval_min, DEAD past 3x). skills/nightly-schedule-canary/schedule-canary.mjs reads every registry entry tagged "kind":"nightly-workflow" and pages (via setup/page-on-failure.mjs, same as every other nightly monitor) if any has gone LATE/DEAD; it is itself run as a step inside .github/workflows/nightly-fleet-sentinels.yml, deliberately NOT folded into drift-sentinel.mjs's own --strict (drift-sentinel's other two sub-checks, image-drift and drift-recon, carry real pre-existing findings unrelated to this task; flipping drift-sentinel itself to --strict would page on those instead of on schedule-staleness). The other 6 nightly-workflow entries below share this exact design; see this entry for the full rationale.
